source: Montague, Dayan, Sejnowski (1996) A framework for mesencephalic dopamine systems based on predictive Hebbian learning
finding: Proposed that dopamine neuron firing above or below baseline carries errors in cortical reward predictions, built with temporal difference (TD) learning. Dopamine acts on synaptic plasticity to correct predictions. The model also makes predictions about human choice on a simple task.
numbers: No numbers read this session (abstract only).
quote: We develop a theoretical framework that shows how mesencephalic dopamine systems could distribute to their targets a signal that represents information about future expectations.
limits: Only the abstract was read (Europe PMC). Theory, not data.
agent_relevance: The TD error is a local learning signal that changes stored values. A prompted LLM has no such signal inside one run, so this theory sits outside the thinking loop.

source: Schultz, Dayan, Montague (1997) A neural substrate of prediction and reward
finding: Joined monkey dopamine recordings with TD learning. Dopamine neurons signal changes or errors in predictions of future rewarding events, and the findings fit quantitative theories of adaptive optimizing control.
numbers: No numbers read this session (abstract only).
limits: Only the abstract was read. The classic three-case pattern (burst for unpredicted reward, no change for fully predicted reward, dip for omitted predicted reward) is background knowledge, not verified here.
agent_relevance: Defines the target quantity: delta = r + gamma*V(next) - V(now). A clean definition of surprise relative to expectation.

source: Bayer and Glimcher (2005) Midbrain dopamine neurons encode a quantitative reward prediction error signal
finding: Single monkey dopamine neurons, in a learned eye-movement-for-juice task, encoded current reward minus a weighted average of previous rewards, but only for outcomes better than expected. The signal kept being computed even when behaviour was only weakly driven by it.
numbers: No numbers read this session (abstract only).
quote: these neurons encoded the difference between the current reward and a weighted average of previous rewards, a reward prediction error, but only for outcomes that were better than expected.
limits: Encoding limited to positive errors. The low baseline firing rate leaves little room for negative errors (see Hart 2014 for release data).
agent_relevance: The expectation is a recency-weighted average. An agent can flag surprise against a running average of past outcomes.

source: Tobler, Fiorillo, Schultz (2005) Adaptive coding of reward value by dopamine neurons
finding: Dopamine responses shifted relative to the expected reward value and the gain adjusted to the variance of reward value, so sensitivity stays high across a wide range of rewards.
numbers: No numbers read this session (abstract only).
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Error signals are scaled by expected spread. An agent comparing surprise across tasks should normalise by the spread of past outcomes.

source: Nakahara et al. (2004) Dopamine neurons can represent context-dependent prediction error
finding: In monkeys, the dopamine response to a reward-indicating light rose with the number of preceding unrewarded trials in a fixed-probability task, as a conventional TD model predicts. In a task where reward probability rose with each unrewarded trial the correlation reversed, and only a TD model with context could simulate it.
numbers: No numbers read this session (abstract only).
limits: Abstract only. Shows plain TD is not enough; the state representation matters.
agent_relevance: The state definition decides what counts as a surprise. The context fed to the expectation must be chosen well.

source: Daw, Gershman, Seymour, Dayan, Dolan (2011) Model-based influences on humans' choices and striatal prediction errors
finding: Two-stage choice task in fMRI. Choices mixed model-free and model-based strategies. Ventral striatal prediction-error BOLD signals were not pure model-free TD errors; they also reflected model-based values.
numbers: 17 healthy adults (5 female, mean age 25.8). 201 trials in three blocks of 67. Reward probabilities drifted by Gaussian noise (SD 0.025, bounds .25 to .75). Median model-free weight 61% (model-based 39%), different from 0 and 100% (sign tests, P<.005). Across-subject neural vs behavioural model-based weight correlated in right ventral striatum (p<.01, small-volume corrected).
quote: These results challenge the notion of a separate model-free learner and suggest a more integrated computational architecture for high-level human decision-making.
limits: Small sample. BOLD is slow and indirect, so it does not show that dopamine neurons themselves carry model-based errors.
agent_relevance: Core challenge to a pure model-free dopamine story. Expect value signals that already blend learned history with a model of the task.

source: Daw et al. (2011) - the stay-probability signature
finding: Behavioural test: does a reward on trial n after a common versus rare transition change the chance of repeating the first-stage choice on trial n+1? Pure model-free predicts a reward effect regardless of transition; model-based predicts a reward-by-transition interaction. Behaviour showed both.
numbers: Same 17 subjects. Hybrid algorithm fit with weighting parameter w and eligibility parameter lambda.
limits: The task became the standard two-step task. Later large-sample re-examinations of what it isolates were not read this session.
agent_relevance: A usable design for testing an LLM: it separates retrospective chaining from forward planning. Demircan 2024 runs it on Llama.

source: Daw et al. (2011) - model-free RPE regressor and difference regressor logic
finding: To test the purity of striatal RPEs, BOLD was regressed on the model-free TD RPE and on the difference between a hybrid RPE and the model-free one. If the signal were pure model-free, the difference regressor would add nothing. It did add: right ventral striatum and vmPFC reflected valuations computed partly by model-based methods.
numbers: Neural and behavioural model-based weights correlated across subjects in right ventral striatum (p<.01, small-volume corrected within bilateral nucleus accumbens mask), overlapping the basic RPE site.
limits: fMRI cannot separate afferent input from local processing.
agent_relevance: Method pattern: test a theory's purity by adding a rival regressor. The same pattern can test whether an agent's surprise is explained by simple repetition alone.

source: Doll, Simon, Daw (2012) The ubiquity of model-based reinforcement learning
finding: Reviews why model-based signatures appear in the same striatal and dopamine-linked regions once thought to be model-free. Frames model-free vs model-based as the computational version of habit vs goal-directed behaviour, tested with revaluation probes.
numbers: Review, no new sample. Notes that pharmacological dopamine blockade left goal-directed instrumental learning unaffected at doses that affected (presumably model-free) Pavlovian conditioning, while human studies hint at a dopamine role in goal-directed behaviour.
quote: Puzzlingly, signatures from these computations seem to be pervasive in the very same regions previously thought to support model-free learning.
limits: A 2012 review; the picture has moved (see Sharpe 2017, 2020). Only the introduction and goals-and-habits section were read closely.
agent_relevance: The assigned key work. Model-free learning is not separable from a world model in the brain; learning (outside the loop) still interacts with planning (inside the loop).

source: Doll et al. (2012) - goals vs habits and revaluation
finding: Model-free RL reinvents Thorndike's law of effect. Model-based RL learns transition structure and plans by simulation. The diagnostic is revaluation: if behaviour adjusts at once to a devalued outcome, it is goal-directed.
numbers: Not numeric. Cited human work on levodopa and Parkinson disease and habit vs goal-directed control (de Wit 2011, 2012) was not opened.
limits: Cited studies not opened.
agent_relevance: Sets the vocabulary: a reasoning loop is model-based planning by definition; RPE learning is the cached-value part.

source: Hart, Rutledge, Glimcher, Phillips (2014) Phasic dopamine release in the rat nucleus accumbens symmetrically encodes a reward prediction error term
finding: Fast-scan cyclic voltammetry in rat nucleus accumbens core during a probabilistic task: dopamine release carried a bidirectional RPE with symmetric scaling of positive and negative errors.
numbers: Only the abstract was retrieved; no sample size read.
quote: dopamine concentrations transmit a bidirectional RPE signal with symmetrical encoding of positive and negative RPEs.
limits: Challenges the view that low spike rates limit negative error coding, but release is not spiking.
agent_relevance: Negative surprise (omission) may deserve the same weight as positive surprise in an agent's update rule.

source: Eshel, Tian, Bukwich, Uchida (2016) Dopamine neurons share common response function for reward prediction error
finding: Mouse VTA dopamine neurons, light-identified, showed responses that are scaled copies of one function across neurons. Expectation acted as a scaled subtraction on the reward response.
numbers: Light-identified dopamine neurons: n=40 (variable-reward task), n=31 (variable-expectation task). Putative dopamine neurons: n=44 and n=28. Noise correlations in 114 neuron pairs. Results qualitatively the same for identified and putative cells.
limits: Mice, one odor-reward task family. Dabney 2020 later re-examined the common-function claim and argued for diversity.
agent_relevance: Baseline version of the theory: one scalar error shared across neurons.

source: Dabney, Kurth-Nelson, Uchida, et al. (2020) A distributional code for value in dopamine-based reinforcement learning
finding: Distributional TD: neurons have different positive and negative learning rates, so they predict different points of the reward distribution. Reanalysis of mouse VTA data found diverse reversal points and asymmetries that correlate across cells.
numbers: Variable-magnitude task: n=40 cells from 5 animals (3, 6, 9, 16, 6 per animal). Reversal-point split-half reliability R=0.58, p=1.8e-5. At the 5 uL reward, 13/40 cells were above baseline and 10/40 below. Asymmetry vs reversal point: p=8.1e-5 (p=0.002 in the single animal with most cells). Second dataset: diversity ANOVA F(14,90)=4.06, p=2e-5; variable-probability task n=31 cells from 5 animals.
limits: Reanalysis of existing data, small cell counts, mouse VTA only. Later work (Avvisati 2024) found extra structure by projection target.
agent_relevance: Distributional value is an AI idea (distributional RL) feeding back into neuroscience. For an LLM agent: keep a spread of outcomes, not only the mean.

source: Dabney et al. (2020) - extended-data control panels
finding: Extended-data captions report control analyses where reversal points estimated in two independent partitions did not correlate, and asymmetry did not relate to reversal point, in a comparison data set built to lack diversity.
numbers: p=0.32 (partition correlation) and p=0.78 (asymmetry vs reversal point), by linear regression.
limits: Only the caption text was read; these panels look like null comparisons, not failed replications of the main result.
agent_relevance: Shows the main claim was stress-tested against a same-reversal-point alternative.

source: Sharpe, Chang, Liu, et al. (2017) Dopamine transients are sufficient and necessary for acquisition of model-based associations
finding: Using sensory preconditioning plus blocking in rats, artificial VTA dopamine activation at the C-to-X transition reversed blocking of the C-X association with no reward and no value. Suppressing dopamine at that transition impaired normal stimulus-stimulus learning. So dopamine errors also drive learning of value-free associations.
numbers: ChR2 n=18, eYFP n=19 rats. Group x cue interaction F(1,35)=4.154, p=0.049. C vs D difference in ChR2: F(1,35)=8.52, p=0.006; in eYFP: F(1,35)=0.006, p=0.940. Responding to C higher in ChR2 than eYFP: F(1,35)=5.277, p=0.028.
quote: These results establish that the acquisition of model-based information about transitions between non-rewarding events is also driven by prediction errors.
limits: Rats; optogenetic stimulation is non-physiological in timing and strength. The interaction p=0.049 is borderline.
agent_relevance: Prediction errors in the brain teach world models, not only values. A scaffold that only updates a value estimate misses half the signal.

source: Sharpe et al. (2017) - sensory preconditioning design
finding: Blocking applied to value-free learning: cue C predicts X during preconditioning, with a prior A-X pairing blocking it. Light-evoked dopamine at X on AC trials restored learning about C. Responding to D served as a control.
numbers: Conditioning day effect F(3,105)=39.71, p<0.0001; no group main effect (F(1,35)=0.553, p=0.46) and no group x day interaction (F(3,105)=0.13, p=0.94).
limits: Rats only.
agent_relevance: Prediction-error-gated learning can apply to non-reward links, hinting that agents could gate memory writes by surprise about transitions, not only about rewards.

source: Sharpe, Batchelor, Mueller, et al. (2020) Dopamine transients do not act as model-free prediction errors during associative learning
finding: In three experiments, optogenetic activation of dopamine neurons during associative learning did not give antecedent cues value. The cues instead became associated with the later events, whether valueless cues or valued rewards. This argues against the model-free reading of dopamine transients.
numbers: Experiment 1: ChR2 n=8, eYFP n=8 rats. A later experiment: ChR2 n=14, eYFP n=14. Light: 1 s, 473 nm, 20 Hz, 16 to 18 mW.
quote: In learning situations appropriate for the appearance of a prediction error, dopamine transients support associative, rather than model-free, learning.
limits: Rat optogenetics. The authors' reading is contested by Maes 2020.
agent_relevance: A live dispute whether the dopamine signal updates value or teaches associations. For a scaffold, store what follows what as well as how good.

source: Maes, Sharpe, Usypchuk, et al. (2020) Causal evidence supporting the proposal that dopamine transients function as temporal difference prediction errors
finding: Optogenetic shunting of dopamine at the start of a reward-predicting cue prevented second-order conditioning but left blocking intact. That fits cue-evoked transients being TD errors rather than reward predictions.
numbers: NpHR group about 16 rats (df 1,15); eYFP control about 11 (df 1,10), inferred from degrees of freedom. Conditioning to cue A over the first 8 days: NpHR F(1,15)=65.6, p<0.005; eYFP F(1,10)=94.4, p<0.005. Simulations used alpha=0.05, gamma=0.95.
quote: optogenetically-shunting dopamine activity at the start of a reward-predicting cue prevents second-order conditioning without affecting blocking.
limits: Rat study; sample sizes inferred. The result supports TD on one test while Sharpe 2020 argues the other way on another; the field is split.
agent_relevance: The TD reading survives a clean causal test. Supports using delta = r + gamma*V' as the working quantity.

source: Maes et al. (2020) - why second-order conditioning alone is not enough
finding: Design point: shunting dopamine at cue onset could stop second-order learning either by removing the error or by removing the cue's reward-predicting power. Adding a blocking test in the same animals separates the two readings.
numbers: Same rats ran blocking before the second-order experiment.
limits: Within-subject design; the conclusion partly rests on a null effect on blocking.
agent_relevance: Design lesson for agent tests: pair every ablation with a control that separates two explanations of the same drop.

source: Kim, Malik, Mikhael, et al. (2020) A unified framework for dopamine signals across timescales
finding: Mice in virtual reality: slow dopamine ramps toward a goal follow RPE with moment-by-moment value changes, not value itself. Teleport and speed manipulations broke the value account: the phasic response to a teleport exceeded the standard ramp peak.
numbers: Calcium ramping R=0.18 +/- 0.04 (n=16 mice); Pearson r=0.45 on the average trace, 95% CI [0.43, 0.48], p<1e-20. Anticipatory licking developed (n=16, p=0.00043, Wilcoxon). Standard-condition peak ratio 2.25 +/- 0.31, p=0.0010 (n=11 mice). Short-teleport response ratio 1.35.
limits: One virtual-reality design. Other ramp accounts exist and were not read.
agent_relevance: Dopamine reads as a derivative of value over time: change in expectation, which is different from value itself.

source: Jeong, Taylor, Floeder, et al. (2022) Mesolimbic dopamine release conveys causal associations
finding: Proposes ANCCR (adjusted net contingency for causal relations): dopamine signals meaningful causal targets using retrospective associations, not RPE. ANCCR reproduces blocking, unblocking, overexpectation, conditioned inhibition and probability and magnitude responses, but predicts differently on naive-animal reward responses, sequential conditioning and cue2 suppression.
numbers: First test used n=8 mice with dLight 1.3b photometry, sessions of 100 rewards. Cue responses rose over trials rather than showing a backpropagating bump of activity.
quote: ANCCR instead predicts that dopamine responses to both cues will increase together
limits: A competing account, not a consensus. Numbers for the cue2-suppression test were not pulled.
agent_relevance: Alternative to RPE: learning triggered by causal contingency. An agent that stores what caused what mirrors this.

source: Avvisati, Kaufmann, Young, et al. (2024) Distributional coding of associative learning in discrete populations of midbrain dopamine neurons
finding: Single labelled midbrain dopamine neurons during associative behaviour encoded reward and behavioural parameters heterogeneously, and unevenly across populations. Projection-defined groups (DMS vs DLS) conveyed distinct signals. A putative DLS-projecting medial SNc group had no firing increase at reward.
numbers: N=52 neurons from 30 mice. DLS-projecting group n=10 neurons.
limits: Complicates both the uniform-RPE picture and the optimism-by-neuron picture; heterogeneity seems tied to target region.
agent_relevance: A single scalar error may be too simple; different channels may carry different error types.

source: Deserno, Moran, Michely, et al. (2021) Dopamine enhances model-free credit assignment through boosting of retrospective model-based inference
finding: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-subject levodopa study. Levodopa boosted model-based inference guiding model-free credit assignment, without directly changing model-free or model-based influence. The drug effect correlated negatively with a change in purely model-based credit assignment.
numbers: Only the abstract was read; sample size not extracted.
limits: Pharmacological manipulation in humans; dose and N not read.
agent_relevance: Inference about what happened can steer which earlier choice gets credit: a link between planning and learning.

source: Demircan, Saanum, Jagadish, Binz, Schulz (2024) Sparse autoencoders reveal temporal difference learning in large language models
finding: Llama 3 70B solves simple in-context RL tasks. Sparse autoencoders on the residual stream find features matching TD errors and Q-values, though the model was only trained for next-token prediction. Interventions on these features change behaviour.
numbers: Best TD-error SAE feature in block 34 correlates r=0.58 with the TD error of a Q-learning model. SAEs trained with regularisation 1e-05 for 30 epochs on 18000 residual stream representations. Deactivating the TD latent made task performance significantly worse; deactivating the lowest-correlation feature did not.
quote: representations that closely match temporal difference (TD) errors. Notably, these representations emerge despite the model only being trained to predict the next token.
limits: One open-weights model, preprint, simple tasks. r=0.58 is moderate. Correlation with a fitted Q-learning agent is not proof of an actual TD computation.
agent_relevance: The most direct LLM test of the RPE idea. An LLM can carry a TD-like signal in context, so outcome history in the prompt may support value learning without weight updates.

source: Demircan et al. (2024) - the two-step task variants
finding: They ran the two-step task and two variants where either the reward function or the transition function changes mid-run, since such changes cause large positive or negative TD errors. Llama predicts a Q-learning agent's actions better when given correct reward information.
numbers: SAE features tracked myopic reward values and Q-values across transformer blocks, with significant correlations to Q-values and a reward-tracking variable.
limits: Small simulated tasks; no human comparison.
agent_relevance: A ready test bench for scaffold claims: change reward or transition mid-run and see whether the agent updates.

source: Montague et al. (1996) and Schultz et al. (1997) - the TD formalism
finding: TD error delta(t) = r(t) + gamma*V(t+1) - V(t). Dopamine firing is read as delta: burst for positive, dip for negative, cue response when a cue predicts reward.
numbers: Formula is the standard TD(0) definition from background knowledge. Maes 2020 text confirms the form (delta at the cue, V at the reward state) and uses alpha=0.05, gamma=0.95.
limits: Formula not verified from these papers' full text.
agent_relevance: A one-line update rule that can be applied to outcome records in any agent memory.

source: Field trajectory: Doll 2012 to Sharpe 2017, 2020 and Maes 2020
finding: Doll 2012 pointed to model-based signals in model-free regions. Sharpe 2017 showed dopamine drives learning of value-free associations. Sharpe 2020 argued transients are not model-free errors. Maes 2020 argued cue-evoked transients are TD errors on a different test.
numbers: Sharpe 2020: three optogenetic experiments in rats learning with and without reward.
limits: Synthesis line. The Sharpe and Maes papers share an author (Schoenbaum), so part of the dispute sits inside one lab.
agent_relevance: Treat dopamine as model-free RPE as contested; the safe description is a teaching signal for expectation errors.
